summary: Sirach 15 first pictures Wisdom as a woman who receives, feeds, steadies, honors, and gladdens the person who fears the Lord and holds the law. It then contrasts that welcome with fools, sinners, pride, liars, and false praise. The chapter closes by rejecting the claim that God causes sin, insisting that people face real choices while God sees every act.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins two major concerns of Sirach: wisdom is a gift to be pursued through reverence and law, and human beings remain responsible for their choices. It gives a compact account of wisdom, praise, commandment keeping, and moral agency within the book's wider instruction.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora who wanted to live according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with the temple, priesthood, Torah study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean life forming the book's world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in poetic teaching: paired lines, vivid comparisons, direct address, moral contrasts, and practical formation.

outline.heading: Wisdom Receives the Reverent
outline.note: The person who fears the Lord and possesses the law obtains Wisdom, who is pictured as mother, wife, and provider of understanding.

outline.heading: Wisdom Establishes and Honors
outline.note: Wisdom steadies the person who relies on her, opens his mouth in the congregation, and gives joy, gladness, and a lasting name.

outline.heading: Who Does Not Obtain Wisdom
outline.note: Fools, sinners, pride, liars, and empty praise are contrasted with praise spoken in wisdom and prospered by the Lord.

outline.heading: Do Not Blame God for Sin
outline.note: The speaker forbids saying that the Lord caused falling away or error, because the Lord hates abomination and those who fear him do not love such things.

outline.heading: Choice Before God Who Sees
outline.note: Human beings are left in the hand of their own counsel, faced with commandments, fire and water, life and death, while the Lord sees every act and gives no license to sin.

keyVerses.text: He who fears the Lord will do this. He who has possession of the law will obtain her.
keyVerses.why: This verse introduces the chapter's link between fearing the Lord, holding the law, and obtaining Wisdom.

keyVerses.text: She will feed him with bread of understanding and give him water of wisdom to drink.
keyVerses.why: The image makes Wisdom's benefit concrete: she nourishes the learner with understanding and wisdom.

keyVerses.text: If you choose, you can keep the commandments. To be faithful is a matter of your choice.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the chapter's second half, where responsibility and choice are emphasized.

keyVerses.text: He has not commanded any man to be ungodly. He has not given any man license to sin.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse states the chapter's rejection of blaming God for wrongdoing.

themes: Fear of the Lord and the law

questions.question: Who is the “her” that someone obtains?
questions.answer: The chapter speaks of Wisdom as “she” and “her.” Verses 2-6 picture her as a mother, a wife, one who feeds, supports, honors, and gives joy. Sirach often personifies Wisdom, so this is poetic instruction rather than a new human character entering the scene.

questions.question: What does this chapter connect with obtaining Wisdom?
questions.answer: Verse 1 connects obtaining Wisdom with fearing the Lord and having possession of the law. The chapter does not present Wisdom as detached information; it links her to reverence, law, and faithful conduct. That fits Sirach's wider setting as instruction for living wisely according to the law.

questions.question: Why is Wisdom compared to a mother and a wife?
questions.answer: Verse 2 uses family images to show welcome, care, and close belonging. Verse 3 continues the image by saying she feeds the learner with understanding and gives wisdom to drink. The point is not a literal biography of Wisdom, but a vivid way to describe her nearness and benefit.

questions.question: Does the chapter say everyone receives Wisdom?
questions.answer: No. Verses 7-8 say that foolish men will not obtain her, sinners will not see her, and liars will not remember her; Wisdom is also described as far from pride. The chapter draws a moral contrast between the person who fears the Lord and those whose conduct resists Wisdom.

questions.question: What is wrong with praise “in the mouth of a sinner”?
questions.answer: Verse 9 says such praise is “not attractive,” and verse 10 contrasts it with praise spoken in wisdom. The chapter does not explain every case, but it presents praise as something that should fit a wise and truthful life, not merely religious speech from someone persisting in sin.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying God causes people to sin?
questions.answer: No. Verses 11-12 directly reject saying that falling away or error is “through the Lord” or caused by him. Verse 20 closes the point by saying God has not commanded anyone to be ungodly or given anyone license to sin.

questions.question: How does the chapter describe human choice?
questions.answer: It says God made man and left him “in the hand of his own counsel.” It then uses paired images: commandments can be kept, fire and water are set before the person, and life and death stand before man. The language strongly emphasizes responsibility, though readers differ on how to relate this to later debates about grace, freedom, and divine sovereignty.

questions.question: What does “fire and water” mean here?
questions.answer: Verse 16 presents fire and water as a simple contrast of alternatives placed before a person. The next verse explains the direction of the image by naming “life and death.” The chapter uses the image to make choice vivid, not to discuss literal fire or literal water.

questions.question: If people choose, does God stop paying attention?
questions.answer: No. Verses 18-19 say the Lord is wise, powerful, sees all things, watches those who fear him, and knows every act of man. The chapter holds human responsibility together with divine knowledge rather than treating choice as hidden from God.

glossary.def: In this chapter, the law is something a person may possess; verse 1 connects it with obtaining Wisdom.
The gathered community in which Wisdom opens a person's mouth, according to verse 5.
The commands a person can keep if he chooses, according to verse 15.
Permission to do wrong; verse 20 says God has not given this to anyone.
